Tabitha (Dorcas)
TAB-ih-tha (DOR-kas)
proper noun
Tabitha: Aramaic for “gazelle”; Dorcas: Greek translation of the same (also “gazelle”). The female disciple at Joppa famous for her good works and almsdeeds, raised from the dead by Peter in Acts 9:36-43.

📖 Biblical Definition

Tabitha (also called by the Greek translation of her Aramaic name, Dorcas—both meaning “gazelle”) is the female disciple at Joppa whose death-and-resurrection-by-Peter is recorded in Acts 9:36-43, one of the most pastorally substantive minor-character narratives in the early church’s history. The full text spans Acts 9:36-43. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the introduction. Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did. The brief introduction establishes her distinctive characterization: full of good works and almsdeeds. The Greek text uses the cognate forms ergōn agathōn (good works) and eleēmosunōn (acts of mercy, almsdeeds), suggesting a sustained pattern of practical-benevolent ministry. Second, the death-and-mourning. And it came to pass in those days, that she was sick, and died: whom when they had washed, they laid her in an upper chamber. The disciples sent for Peter (who was nearby in Lydda), urging him to come without delay. And all the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them. The detail is significant: Tabitha’s ministry had included clothing-the-widows, and the widows who had been recipients of her practical care now stood weeping over the loss of their benefactor, with the garments she had sewn for them held in their hands as the substantive evidence of her ministry. Third, the resurrection. But Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down, and prayed; and turning him to the body said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up. And he gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive. The Tabitha-resurrection is one of three explicit resurrection-miracles in Acts (with Eutychus in Acts 20 and the more general references to apostolic healings); the substance follows the pattern of Christ’s own resurrection-miracles (compare the daughter of Jairus, Mark 5:41, where Christ said talitha cumi—Aramaic damsel, arise; Peter’s Tabitha, arise is the close apostolic echo). Fourth, the consequence. And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord. The resurrection-miracle produced substantial gospel-fruit: the news spread; many believed. The Tabitha-narrative is therefore one of the most pastorally substantive NT pictures of the practical-benevolent ministry as part of the apostolic-era church’s life—a female disciple whose distinctive characterization was full of good works and almsdeeds, whose specific ministry included clothing-the-widows, whose death produced substantial mourning among the recipients of her care, whose resurrection by Peter brought many to faith in the Lord.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Tabitha (Aramaic, “gazelle”; Greek Dorcas, the same) was the female disciple at Joppa full of good works and almsdeeds, particularly clothing-the-widows; her death-and-resurrection by Peter (Acts 9:36-43) brought substantial gospel-fruit in Joppa and stands as one of the most pastorally substantive NT pictures of the practical-benevolent ministry.

expand to see more

TABITHA — Aramaic name meaning gazelle; the female disciple at Joppa raised from the dead by Peter (Acts 9:36-43).

DORCAS — Greek translation of the Aramaic Tabitha; the same person; the name has subsequently become eponymous of Christian women’s practical-benevolent ministries (Dorcas societies, Dorcas guilds).

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 9:36 — "Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did."

Acts 9:39 — "Then Peter arose and went with them. When he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber: and all the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them."

Acts 9:40-41 — "But Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down, and prayed; and turning him to the body said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up. And he gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive."

Acts 9:42 — "And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Tabitha-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the loss of attention to her as a substantive biblical model of practical-benevolent ministry in much contemporary preaching (which has often passed over Acts 9:36-43 quickly as one resurrection-miracle among several without engaging the substantive characterization of Tabitha’s ministry)—and by the contemporary church’s under-appreciation of the clothing-the-widows-type practical-mercy ministries that Tabitha exemplifies.

expand to see more

The loss of attention to Tabitha as a substantive biblical model of practical-benevolent ministry has dropped her from active discipleship-instruction in much contemporary preaching. Acts 9:36-43’s detailed portrait—Tabitha named, identified as a disciple, characterized as full of good works and almsdeeds, her clothing-the-widows specific ministry detailed, the widows weeping over her with her hand-sewn garments held in evidence—is substantive enough to support a discipleship-model the contemporary church needs. The recovery is the recovery of Tabitha as a substantive model: the female disciple whose distinctive ministry was the practical-benevolent care of the most vulnerable members of the early church (widows, especially), with such substantial fruit that her death produced city-wide mourning and her resurrection produced city-wide conversion. The contemporary church’s preaching often passes over her as a brief incident; recovery is the substantive engagement of her portrait as one of the most pastorally rich female-disciple models in the NT.

The deeper contemporary corruption is the church’s under-appreciation of the clothing-the-widows-type practical-mercy ministries that Tabitha exemplifies. The clothing-the-widows ministry was substantive (Tabitha was sewing actual garments for actual widows over a sustained period, evidenced by the widows producing the garments at her death); it was specific (not generic charitable giving but targeted relief of the named recipients with personal sustained relationship); it was demonstrably gospel-fruitful (Peter’s resurrection-miracle produced substantial conversion in Joppa, building on the church’s established practical-benevolent reputation). The contemporary church often values teaching-and-leadership-ministries over practical-benevolent ministries, with the result that Tabitha-type ministries are under-recognized and under-supported. The recovery is the recovery of the practical-benevolent ministry as substantive gospel-ministry. Subsequent church history has often understood this: the Dorcas societies and Dorcas guilds that took her name in the 18th-and-19th centuries (and that continue in many churches today) carried forward the Tabitha-pattern of organized practical-benevolent ministry, particularly the sewing-for-the-poor ministry that her example specifically anchored. The recovery in the contemporary church is the recovery of the substantive value of such ministries as part of the gospel-witness of the body of Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic Tabithā and Greek Dorkas (both meaning gazelle); the female disciple at Joppa full of good works and almsdeeds, particularly the clothing-the-widows ministry; raised from the dead by Peter (Acts 9:36-43); one of the most pastorally substantive female-disciple models in the NT, with city-wide gospel-fruit following her resurrection.

expand to see more

Greek Tabithā (G5000) — Tabitha (Acts 9:36, 40, the only NT uses).

Greek Dorkas (G1393) — Dorcas (Acts 9:36, 39, the only NT uses; same person as Tabitha).

Greek mathētria (G3102) — female disciple (the only NT use; Acts 9:36; Tabitha is the only person explicitly called mathētria).

Greek eleēmosunē (G1654) — alms, acts of mercy (Acts 9:36, Tabitha’s characteristic ministry).

Usage

"This woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did—Tabitha’s distinctive characterization as the substantive female disciple of practical-benevolent ministry."

"All the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made—the visible evidence of Tabitha’s sustained clothing-the-widows ministry at the moment of her death."

"Loss of attention to Tabitha drops her as a substantive female-disciple model; contemporary under-appreciation of practical-benevolent ministries under-values Tabitha-type service; recovery restores both the substantive narrative and the practical-benevolent ministry as substantive gospel-witness."
